question: A department shares one pooled allowance. Several colleagues have got into the habit of running everyday drafting and tidying-up work on the deepest-reasoning tier because it is available to them. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The department loses track of which tier produced which document, making it harder to reproduce a particular draft afterwards.
B) The routine drafts come back more slowly than they need to, so each colleague spends a little longer waiting for everyday work.
C) Colleagues become accustomed to the deeper tier's style of answer and find the default tier's phrasing harder to work with later.
D) The shared allowance is consumed by low-value work, so it is not there when a colleague has genuinely hard analysis to run.
correct_answers: D) The shared allowance is consumed by low-value work, so it is not there when a colleague has genuinely hard analysis to run.
explanations: Not recording which tier produced a draft is an untidy practice, but it rarely affects the outcome of everyday drafting and does not explain why the allowance is being exhausted.
Slower turnaround on routine drafting is a real irritation and worth avoiding, but a few extra seconds per draft is minor next to the shared pool running dry before the hard work gets done.
Getting used to one tier's phrasing is a mild adjustment, not a risk to the department's work. Everyday drafting is well within what the default tier handles, and preference is not the issue here.

Correct. The deepest tier consumes meaningfully more of a shared allowance, so spending it on work the default tier handles well leaves nothing for the small number of tasks that genuinely need that depth.
